title: Verification, validation and output analysis
subtitle: A simulation gives numbers. These are the checks that say whether to believe them, and how much.

sections.title: Verification versus validation
sections.body: Verification: is the model built right? — does the program faithfully implement the conceptual model (debugging, code walkthroughs, tracing, checking against hand calculations, simple cases with known answers)? Validation: is it the right model? — does it reproduce the real system’s behaviour closely enough for its purpose (comparing with real data, expert review, sensitivity analysis)? Naylor and Finger: build face-valid assumptions, test them, and compare the model’s output with the real system.

sections.title: Calibration and sources of error
sections.body: Calibration adjusts model parameters until the output matches observed data, iterating between model and real system. Errors: wrong assumptions, wrong input distributions, sampling error, programming bugs, truncation. Techniques: the Turing-style test (can experts tell simulated output from real?), extreme-condition tests, sensitivity analysis (vary an input 10% — does the output change sensibly?).

choices.text: An input or parameter slightly and watches how the output responds.

sections.title: Confidence intervals
sections.body: One run is a sample of size one. Simulation output is random, so report a confidence interval around the estimate: x̄ ± z·s/√n (or t for small n). A 95% interval means: if the experiment were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true mean. The demonstration builds 40 intervals from fresh samples; the coverage is 97.5% (expected ≈ 95).

worked.why: 20 replications give a mean wait of 12.0 min with standard deviation 3.0.
95% CI half-width ≈ 1.96·3/√20 (use t₁₉ = 2.09 for small n: 1.40).

sections.title: Why averages are normal: the central limit theorem
sections.body: Whatever the shape of the population, the mean of n independent samples is approximately normal with standard deviation σ/√n. The exponential distribution (σ = 1) is very skewed, yet means of samples of 30 have standard deviation 0.184 against the theoretical 0.183. This is why confidence intervals are valid for simulation averages.

sections.title: Initial bias, replications and run length
sections.body: A simulation starts empty (an empty queue), which is not typical, so early observations are biased — the warm-up or transient period. Remedies: discard an initial segment (Welch's graphical method decides how much), run long enough, or start in a representative state. Independent replications (different seeds) give independent estimates to average; batch means cut one long run into batches and treat batch means as nearly independent.

questions.prompt: The warm-up period is discarded to remove…

choices.text: Bias from the artificial initial conditions.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Steady-state statistics should not include the transient.

problems.prompt: A queue simulation starts empty. Why does its average wait underestimate the steady-state value if the first observations are included?
problems.answer: Early customers find an empty, short queue, so their waits are small; including them pulls the average down. Discarding a warm-up period removes that initial-condition bias.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Verify the code, validate the model, calibrate the parameters.
  • Report confidence intervals; discard warm-up; use replications or batch means.
